presentingComplaint: Found unresponsive at home with an empty pill bottle nearby; witnessed generalized seizure en route to hospital
history: 29-year-old woman with a history of major depressive disorder on amitriptyline 150 mg/day, brought in by ambulance after her roommate found her unresponsive on the bathroom floor with an empty bottle of amitriptyline (previously containing approximately 50 tablets of 50 mg each) and a suicide note. Last seen normal approximately 2 hours earlier. Paramedics witnessed a single generalized tonic-clonic seizure lasting under 2 minutes during transport, which broke spontaneously. No history of co-ingestion reported by roommate, though empty wine glass was also found at scene. No known cardiac disease. No prior overdose attempts documented.
examination: Drowsy, responds only to painful stimuli (GCS 9), intermittent myoclonic jerks. Pupils dilated (6mm), sluggishly reactive. Dry mucous membranes and flushed, dry skin. Absent bowel sounds. Diffusely hyperreflexic early in course. No focal neurological deficit. No signs of trauma. Skin warm and dry, no diaphoresis.

contraindications: Avoid class Ia (procainamide, quinidine) and class Ic antiarrhythmics — additive sodium-channel blockade, can worsen QRS widening and precipitate arrest
Avoid flumazenil if co-ingestion with benzodiazepine suspected — can precipitate seizures in TCA overdose
Avoid physostigmine — historically used but contraindicated due to risk of asystole/seizures in TCA toxicity
Avoid routine gastric lavage beyond early presentation window; airway must be protected first given depressed sensorium
edgeCases: QRS >100ms and terminal R wave in aVR are more predictive of seizure/arrhythmia risk than measured drug level; do not wait for TCA level to act
Serum alkalinization with sodium bicarbonate is the cornerstone treatment for wide QRS/hypotension/arrhythmia, targeting arterial pH 7.50-7.55, independent of presenting pH
Refractory hypotension despite bicarbonate and fluids may require IV lipid emulsion or vasopressors (norepinephrine preferred over dopamine)
Recurrent seizures should be treated with benzodiazepines first-line; avoid phenytoin due to additional sodium-channel blocking effects that may worsen cardiotoxicity

TCA overdose is not one of the reference D1 diagnosable conditions in this build; mapped here to the closest available engine categories (drug_intox as primary; serotonin_nms and seizure_epilepsy as differential proxies) for regression purposes only — acceptableIds intentionally left as [] to avoid false-positive scoring against an unlisted condition
Clinical deterioration can be delayed and rapid; patients require continuous cardiac monitoring for at least 6 hours after any QRS widening or arrhythmia, even if asymptomatic on arrival
